newsitem.title: HUNGARY: NATO's Joulwan hails tough Western stand on Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: NATO's Joulwan hails tough Western stand on Bosnia.

text.p: NATO's Supreme Allied Commander in Europe General George Joulwan welcomed on Tuesday the tough new stance of Western governments towards the former warring factions in Bosnia.

NATO foreign ministers of the Bosnia Peace Implementation Council meeting last week in Sintra, in Portugal, threatened all sides with punitive measures, including action against anyone "harbouring" Bosnia's indicted war criminals, unless they complied with the Dayton peace agreement signed 18 months ago.
"I really think the Sintra conference...reinforced what we've been saying all along," Joulwan told Reuters after meeting Hungarian Prime Minister Gyula Horn.
"Let us really have clear objectives and clear dates of meeting those deadlines and putting the pressure on the parties themselves the former warring factions."
Joulwan mentioned opening up Bosnia's airports and borders as a priority but also looked forward to progress in apprehending war criminals.
"This political will (to track down war criminals) is being developed now within the international community," he said.
Joulwan said he had not yet received new orders to pursue the war criminals more actively.
"Right now I'm operating under the same guidelines that I have received in the past,' he said, adding that the political parties in Bosnia appeared to want to do more on this matter.
"I'm delighted to hear that," he said.
"We are clearly supporting all of that momentum and I would hope that would continue over the next year," he said.

Four years after it was set up by the U.N. Security Council, a war crimes tribunal at The Hague has indicted 75 people, including forner Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and his army commander General Ratko Mladic. But only nine people have been sent to The Hague for prosecution.
Under the Dayton accords, Bosnia is supposed to be a single state with two separate entities, one for Serbs and the other a Croat-Moslem federation.

But Bosnia's ethnic factions have resisted integration, many refugees have been prevented from returning home and the inter-ethnic central government has ignored some of the main provisions of the U.S.-brokered treaty.
Joulwan was speaking during a stopover in Hungary on what he called a "farewell tour" of 20 capitals ahead of his retirement as NATO Supreme Allied Commander on July 10.
Earlier he received Hungary's highest honour that may be bestowed on a non-head of state, the Order of Merit Middle Cross with Star.
